To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
older people are more emotionally stable and mature, and less emotionally reactive, than younger people.

older adults (a) have higher emotional control, mood stabilization, and emotional maturity, (b) have lower levels of emotional intensity (surgency), physiological reactivity, and sensation seeking, (c) experience fewer negative emotions and more positive emotions, (d) have more positive and less negative emotional memories, (e) experience less negative emotion in response to negative events, (f) experience more negative emotions in response to positive events, and (g) are more likely to experience positive emotion
older adults are higher in emotional control and emotional maturity and lower in surgent emotionality and sensation seeking than middle-aged or young adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theory of emotional development that emphasizes the self-regulation of emotion.
the development of a theory of emotion that is consistent with the developmental perspective and with the study of the development of self-regulation of affect.
the development and application of a model of the dimensions of affective experience.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are age-related differences in the dimensions of affective experience, which may be due to developmental changes or cohort-related differences.
the dimensions of affect are complex, multidimensional, and multifunctional.
there is some evidence for age differences in emotional experience, but the evidence does not yet support any specific conclusions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

affective experience in the elderly is more complex, more integrated, less reactive, and less intense than in the middle aged and young adults, with the middle-aged group falling somewhere between the extremes.
affective experience in the aged is characterized by a greater capacity to regulate emotion.
age-related changes in emotion are complex and multidimensional.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have a good idea of how emotions change with age.
the dimensions of emotional experience are not static, but rather are malleable and can change over time.
there are important differences in the way that people experience and regulate emotion across the adult lifespan.
